findings.title: The PR increases the cadence of every cleanup job by tenfold
findings.body: Changing the shared cleanup ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute affects much more than annotation cleanup: snapshot, dashboard-version, image, temporary-file, short-URL, invite, and query-history cleanup all now run ten times as often. These jobs perform database scans/deletes and the whole cleanup run may take up to the 9-minute timeout; when a run approaches that timeout, the 1-minute ticker is already pending and the next run starts immediately. This can turn expensive cleanup into near-continuous background load. Restore the previous cadence or schedule the annotation job separately if it needs a different interval.

findings.title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors with the complete ID list
findings.body: This call, and the analogous calls at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579, use Error even when err is nil and include the entire ids slice. Every normal cleanup batch therefore produces false error-level events, which can trigger error alerts and generate very large log records (especially with the newly supported 32K-sized batches). Log only aggregate counts at Debug/Info and emit Error only when the select or delete actually fails.

findings.title: Building SQLite ID lists performs quadratic string allocation
findings.body: For SQLite batches over 999, each iteration formats the complete accumulated values string again. The final SQL text for a 32,767-ID batch is hundreds of kilobytes, but this loop repeatedly copies all prior content and can allocate several gigabytes cumulatively. The new 40K-row test exercises this path, and orphan-tag cleanup can hit it as well. Build the list with strings.Builder or a byte slice/strconv.AppendInt so each ID is appended once.

findings.title: Non-SQLite deletes can exceed database bind-parameter limits
findings.body: The non-SQLite path creates one bound parameter for every fetched ID and does not cap or chunk the list. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configurable; values above 65,535 will fail on PostgreSQL/MySQL prepared statements (and lower limits apply to some supported dialects), causing every cleanup run to fail. The old delete subquery did not bind an ID per row. Split ids into dialect-safe chunks, or validate and enforce a conservative maximum batch size.

findings.title: The renamed second-run test no longer performs a second cleanup run
findings.body: This subtest now creates a fresh set of nine annotations, already exactly three per annotation type, and invokes the cleaner only once. Its zero-affected assertion only proves that an already compliant dataset is untouched; it no longer verifies the stated behavior of rerunning max-count cleanup after a preceding run has removed excess annotations. Run the cleaner twice within this subtest and assert that only the second invocation affects zero rows.
